title: The Inventory Doctrine
subtitle: How supply chain and manufacturing theory treated inventory before 2019, what COVID broke, and why the KPIs and risk models changed

measured_series.note: Independent, fixed-schedule public series. These carry the argument; everything else is supporting.

GSCPI.name: Global Supply Chain Pressure Index
GSCPI.source: Federal Reserve Bank of New York
GSCPI.units: standard deviations from the index's own long-run average
GSCPI.vintage_caveat: The index is periodically re-estimated; figures here are the August 2026 vintage. Earlier vintages place the December 2021 peak slightly differently (c. 4.49).
GSCPI.composition: Ocean and air freight cost indices plus PMI delivery-time, backlog and purchased-stocks sub-indices.

inventories_to_sales.name: Manufacturing and Trade Inventories and Sales (MTIS), inventories-to-sales ratio
inventories_to_sales.source: US Census Bureau, retrieved via FRED
inventories_to_sales.units: months of inventory at the current sales rate, seasonally adjusted, current dollars
inventories_to_sales.coverage_in_report: 2018-01 to 2026-06 (chart); full series from 1992-01 used for records and baselines
inventories_to_sales.why_this_series: Numerator and denominator are both in current dollars, so the ratio is largely insulated from the price-level change that makes raw 2019 and 2026 inventory values incomparable.
inventories_to_sales.caveat: April 2020 spikes (total 1.74, manufacturers 1.88, retail 1.68) are a collapse in the denominator — sales stopped — not a build in stock.
inventories_to_sales.baseline_note: Three pre-COVID baselines are reported because the manufacturing result is sensitive to the choice: manufacturing inventories were already climbing through 2019 (1.40 in January to 1.52 in December) under the trade war. The robust claim is the DIVERGENCE between manufacturing and retail, not the size of manufacturing's own increase.

divergence_manufacturing_minus_retail.note: The robust finding. Gap between the two sectors' ratios, then vs now.

the_long_arc.finding: The great compression belongs to the 1990s and early 2000s, not to the 2010s. Manufacturing hit its all-time low of 1.14 in December 2005 and drifted up for fifteen years. Retail bottomed at an annual mean of 1.350 in 2011 and was 8.5% higher (1.464) by 2019. Neither sector was still leaning when the pandemic arrived, so 'COVID ended thirty years of relentless inventory reduction' is not what the data shows.
the_long_arc.note_on_2018_19: The manufacturing climb through 2018-19 lines up with the Section 301 tariffs, not with anything pandemic-related. This is why the baseline choice in the main finding matters.

china_import_share.name: China's share of US goods imports
china_import_share.source: US Census Bureau trade data via FRED (IMPCH / BOPGIMP), annual sums of monthly values
china_import_share.units: percent of total US goods imports
china_import_share.verified: Recomputed independently from the primary FRED series, 28 Aug 2026
china_import_share.finding: Between 2019 and 2022 — the peak years of supply-chain-resilience rhetoric — China's share moved only 17.9% to 16.4%, and absolute imports rose to a record $536.3bn. The collapse came in 2023-2025 and tracks tariff policy. Diversification happened, but it was substantially legislated rather than chosen.

inventory_gdp_swing.name: Contribution of the change in private inventories to real GDP growth
inventory_gdp_swing.source: US Bureau of Economic Analysis via FRED (A014RY2Q224SBEA)
inventory_gdp_swing.units: percentage points of annualised real GDP growth
inventory_gdp_swing.verified: Recomputed independently from the primary FRED series, 28 Aug 2026
inventory_gdp_swing.finding: The 2025 tariff front-run and unwind produced the most violent inventory swing in the US national accounts outside the pandemic itself — a bullwhip, in 2025, among firms that had spent four years saying they had fixed the bullwhip.

survey_series.caveat: Separate waves, different samples, question wording shifts between years — the 2023 dual-sourcing figure is specific to critical raw materials. Directional only; NOT a matched panel.

known_weaknesses: The manufacturing result is baseline-sensitive: manufacturing inventories were already climbing through 2019, so 'manufacturers hold more than before COVID' is true against a multi-year average (+0.08) and false against December 2019 alone (-0.04). All three baselines are reported rather than the flattering one.
Sector-level inventory ratios average over large firm-level variation; a flat sector can hide firms moving in opposite directions.
Survey waves are not a matched panel, so year-on-year movements are indicative rather than measured change.
The KPI ledger describes practice at large, well-resourced firms; the median manufacturer has adopted far less of it.
Framework attributions are conventional rather than uncontested; dates are for the canonical publication, not the first idea.

The corporate DIO and disclosure-language analyses are original work from SEC data, not published series; the DIO result is sensitive to XBRL tag choice and the 10-K text search measures language rather than practice.

corporate_inventory_days.name: Days Inventory Outstanding, balanced panel of 471 large US SEC filers
corporate_inventory_days.source: Own analysis of SEC XBRL company facts (InventoryNet / CostOfGoodsAndServicesSold)
corporate_inventory_days.type: original analysis, not a published series
corporate_inventory_days.caveat: Sensitive to which XBRL cost tag a filer uses: the CostOfRevenue-tag population does show a rise (47.9 in 2019 to 54.2 in 2025). Read as 'no large durable increase at the top', not 'nothing changed anywhere'. The dollar-weighted and equal-weighted answers genuinely differ, which is why single-number claims about corporate inventory are unreliable.

disclosure_language.source: Own analysis, SEC EDGAR full-text search
disclosure_language.caveat: Measures disclosure language, not practice. A firm can dual-source without using the phrase.
disclosure_language.note: Roughly 7,000 annual filers. Set against 81% of executives reporting dual-sourcing programmes.

safety_stock_formula.attribution: Hadley & Whitin; carried into practice via Silver, Pyke & Peterson, and King (2009)

four_compounding_reasons_the_buffer_was_.cause: sigma_L estimated from a calm regime
four_compounding_reasons_the_buffer_was_.evidence: GSCPI 1998-2019 SD 0.494, max +1.58; Dec 2021 +4.44 = 9.0x that SD and 2.8x the entire pre-2020 range
four_compounding_reasons_the_buffer_was_.verified: Recomputed from the NY Fed series, 28 Aug 2026

four_compounding_reasons_the_buffer_was_.cause: the lead-time term is quadratic in mean demand
four_compounding_reasons_the_buffer_was_.evidence: On a representative high-volume part, lead-time variance is 77% of total variance at sigma_L = 3 days and 98% at 12 days
The formula adds variances assuming independence; in 2021 demand and lead-time shocks were positively correlated, biasing the buffer downward
For lognormal lead-time demand at CV 0.50, the true buffer is +14.9% at p95, +44.8% at p99, +84.5% at p99.9

littles_law.note: A distribution-free identity. Holding throughput constant, flow time 8 -> 20 weeks raises pipeline inventory 2.5x with no behavioural change. Explains a large part of the 2021 build that was reported as a strategy shift.

ttr_tts_formalisation.note: TTR is an input to a linear program run once per single-node failure; TTS is the same program with duration as a decision variable, maximised. Robustness criterion: TTS(j) >= TTR(j) for all nodes j. Risk Exposure Index = PI(j) / max_k PI(k).
ttr_tts_formalisation.key_empirical_finding: Risk exposure is uncorrelated with procurement spend: low-value single-sourced parts repeatedly carried the highest impact.
ttr_tts_formalisation.source: Schmidt, Simchi-Levi et al., Interfaces (2015); Simchi-Levi, Schmidt & Wei, HBR (2014)

m5_competition.scale: 42,840 Walmart series, 12 aggregation levels, 9 quantiles, h=28

capacity_as_an_option.source: Cirrus Logic FY2022 Form 10-K; ratio computed from disclosed figures

what_did_not_change: Newsvendor critical fractile Q* = F^-1(cu/(cu+co)) — untouched; the probabilistic-forecasting shift replaces the ESTIMATOR of F, not the rule.
EOQ Q* = sqrt(2DK/h) — untouched, and insensitive: a 100% error in D produces a 41% error in Q*.
Little's Law L = lambda*W — an identity, holds in every regime.
modelling.adoption_not_theory: Clark & Scarf multi-echelon 1960; Little's Law 1961; proper scoring rules long settled; CVaR made tractable by Rockafellar & Uryasev 2000. The bottleneck was adoption, not theory.

corrections_from_adversarial_review.claim_as_originally_written: Every model treats uncertainty as demand-side; supply is assumed reliable.
corrections_from_adversarial_review.correction: True of the practitioner stack (EOQ, classical safety stock, MRP/DRP lead-time offsets, SCOR metrics, ABC/XYZ) but false of pre-2019 inventory THEORY: random-yield, supply-disruption and stochastic-capacity models all predate 2019. The defensible and stronger claim is that supply-side uncertainty was well theorised by 2019 and almost entirely absent from the formulas shipped in planning software, the parameters planners could set, and the metrics anyone was measured on.
corrections_from_adversarial_review.action: Section 1's premise callout rewritten to the narrower claim; it now matches section 6's 'adoption was the bottleneck, not theory'.

corrections_from_adversarial_review.claim_as_originally_written: Inventories-to-sales is insulated from inflation because both terms are in current dollars.
corrections_from_adversarial_review.correction: Inventories are carried at cost and sales booked at selling price, so a gross-margin change moves the ratio with no change in physical stocking; it also moves on mix.
corrections_from_adversarial_review.action: Caveat added to section 8; the argument leans on the sector DIVERGENCE and on three corroborating series with different denominators.

corrections_from_adversarial_review.correction: Wave sizes are small (n=71 in 2021, n=113 in 2022, n=101 in 2023) and the two 78% figures could not be located in any primary exhibit.
corrections_from_adversarial_review.action: Sourcing warning in section 7 strengthened with wave sizes; no conclusion rests on these figures.

corrections_from_adversarial_review.claim_as_originally_written: Inventory is the first of Ohno's seven wastes.
corrections_from_adversarial_review.correction: Overproduction is first, and Ohno singles it out as the root waste that generates the others. Inventory is conventionally fifth.
corrections_from_adversarial_review.action: TPS card corrected. The corrected version actually serves the argument better: inventory is a consequence of overproduction, which is precisely the 'stock is a symptom' reading.

corrections_from_adversarial_review.claim_as_originally_written: Retail spent thirty years proving it could operate on less stock.
corrections_from_adversarial_review.correction: Retail's I/S fell to an annual mean of 1.350 in 2011 and then ROSE 8.5% to 1.464 by 2019. All of retail's decline happened before 2011; there was no retail leaning in the 2010s.
corrections_from_adversarial_review.action: Wording fixed, and a new 1992-2026 long-arc figure added at the top of section 3 so the reader can see the whole record rather than the 2018-2026 close-up alone.

corrections_from_adversarial_review.claim_as_originally_written: Disruption was not measured at all before 2019 — there was no financial metric for it.
corrections_from_adversarial_review.correction: Supply-chain value-at-risk existed as SCOR AG.1.4 from Revision 11.0 (2012), adapting J.P. Morgan's RiskMetrics VaR (1994). It failed not from absence but because VaR = P x Impact requires a probability that does not exist for rare high-impact events — so the standard demoted it to a Level-2/3 diagnostic and practitioners did not produce it.
corrections_from_adversarial_review.action: Ledger row 13 rewritten. The old column is now 'supply-chain value-at-risk (SCOR AG.1.4, in the standard since 2012)' and the failure mode is the missing probability term. This makes the TTR/TTS replacement sharper: it achieves the same ambition by deleting the impossible input.

corrections_from_adversarial_review.claim_as_originally_written: Walmart inventory up 33% year on year in Q1 2022.
corrections_from_adversarial_review.correction: 33.4% is the Walmart U.S. SEGMENT figure from the earnings deck's segment page. CONSOLIDATED inventory rose 32.0% ($61,229m vs $46,383m).
corrections_from_adversarial_review.action: Timeline now states 32% consolidated, with the US segment figure noted separately.

corrections_from_adversarial_review.claim_as_originally_written: Toyota weathered the chip shortage because of its post-Tohoku buffers.
corrections_from_adversarial_review.correction: The post-Tohoku RESCUE database and buffer policy are real and bought months of insulation through early 2021, but by August 2021 Toyota was announcing a roughly 40% cut to September global production on chip and COVID grounds.
corrections_from_adversarial_review.action: The just-in-time steel-man now says the buffer bought time, not immunity, and names the 40% cut.

corrections_from_adversarial_review.claim_as_originally_written: (implicit) the chip shortage was a shortage of chips.
corrections_from_adversarial_review.verdict: ADDED — the record contradicts the framing
corrections_from_adversarial_review.correction: 2021 semiconductor unit shipments hit an all-time record of 1.15 trillion on record revenue of $555.9bn. There was no aggregate shortage; there was an allocation failure.
corrections_from_adversarial_review.action: New callout in section 2, verified independently against the Semiconductor Industry Association.

pre_2019.body: Supply Chain Council (1996), merged into APICS 2014, now ASCM
pre_2019.structure: Five performance attributes: Reliability, Responsiveness, Agility, Cost, Asset Management
pre_2019.risk_treatment: Present only as AG.1.4 Overall Value at Risk, which the standard itself relegated to a Level-2/3 diagnostic because it could not be rolled into cost
pre_2019.inventory_treatment: Appears only through cash-to-cash and return on working capital — capital to be minimised, never capability to be sized

post_2022.version: SCOR Digital Standard v14.0, released September 2022, still current in the 2025 reissue
post_2022.change: Rebuilt around three strategic categories with 'Resilience' named as a first-class category, plus eight sustainability Level-1 metrics
post_2022.honest_caveat: 'Resilience' is a relabelling of the three pre-existing customer-facing attributes, not new measurement. There is still NO Level-1 metric for time-to-survive, single-source exposure, n-tier coverage, disruption-scenario service or inventory composition. Firms running those measures are extending beyond the standard, not implementing it.

ford_risk_exposure_case.source: Simchi-Levi, Schmidt, Wei et al., INFORMS Wagner Prize presentation 2014; Interfaces 45(5), 2015
ford_risk_exposure_case.why_it_matters: A well-resourced supply chain function was watching substantially the wrong sites, because the allocation had been made on spend. Risk exposure turned out to be uncorrelated with procurement spend.
ford_risk_exposure_case.caveat: The raw figures are verified; avoid the 'watching the wrong two-thirds' gloss, which the arithmetic does not support.

hendricks_singhal.source: Hendricks & Singhal, JOM 21(5) 2003; POM 14(1) 2005; and the operating-performance study
hendricks_singhal.three_year_BHAR: -40.66% mean, -59.94% median (N=827); ~67% of firms underperformed their matched portfolio
hendricks_singhal.equity_volatility: +13.50% abnormal change in equity standard deviation in the year after, significant at 1%; does not revert
hendricks_singhal.operating_performance: Control-adjusted: -107% operating income, -114% return on sales, -92% return on assets; also 13.88% higher inventory growth
hendricks_singhal.their_own_diagnosis_of_the_adoption_gap: Efficiency improvement 'is an ongoing activity at most firms, so managers have developed the necessary skills to deal with it, and they know how to justify and manage resources that improve efficiency.' Nobody had those skills for resilience — stated in 2003.

tohoku_deep_tier.renesas: supplied as much as 40% of the world's automotive microcontrollers; at least four months to restore production
tohoku_deep_tier.merck_onahama: the only global source of Xirallic pigment used in metallic car paint
tohoku_deep_tier.point: Neither sat on any carmaker's tier-one risk register, because neither was a tier-one supplier.

no_aggregate_chip_shortage.finding: 2021 was the largest year for semiconductor output in the industry's history — during the shortage.
no_aggregate_chip_shortage.revenue_2021: $555.9bn, up 26.2% year on year, also an all-time record
no_aggregate_chip_shortage.why_it_matters: What failed was not physical capacity but allocation, sequencing and information. A shortage that coexists with record output is a measurement and coordination problem, which is why the response was a new scorecard rather than new factories.

auto_dealer_inventories.series: AISRSA — US auto dealers' inventories-to-sales, US Census via FRED, monthly to July 2026
auto_dealer_inventories.finding: An 84% collapse from the 2015-19 average to the January 2022 trough, and still only 1.36 more than four years later.
auto_dealer_inventories.caveat: The April 2020 reading of 4.34 is a denominator artefact — dealerships shut and sales collapsed.
